name: GGGGS
description: Single flexible Gly-Gly-Gly-Gly-Ser unit — the canonical flexible linker derived from the hinge region of the IgG heavy chain. Widely used for fusing two domains that need independent folding.
priority_reason: The default. Glycine has no side chain to occlude the peptide or to pack against the scaffold, serine keeps the segment soluble, and five residues give a 11-30 aa peptide enough reach to fold on its own while leaving no long protease-accessible tail. Its composition is continuous with the Gly/Ala/Ser repeats of the silk clusters and with the Gly/Pro-rich surface of the collagens, so it is the least likely of the fifteen to disturb the scaffold's own self-assembly. It is also what the stored pipeline rows carry, so accepting the default reproduces the archived assembly instead of departing from it.

name: (GGGGS)₂
description: Two tandem GGGGS units — provides more inter-domain distance and freedom than a single unit while remaining highly soluble. The most used flexible linker length in fusion protein construction.
reference: Chen et al. 2013, Adv Drug Deliv Rev 65(10):1357-1369.
priority_reason: The same chemistry at twice the reach. Use it when the peptide's active region has to clear a large scaffold surface — the collagen clusters here run from 225 to 1071 residues and present a charged, sticky surface that can mask a short peptide — while keeping the peptide free to fold. This is the most widely used flexible-linker length in fusion constructs.

name: KESGS
description: Short flexible linker with one internal K-E salt bridge. Slightly more rigid than GGGGS but still tolerant of inter-domain movement.
priority_reason: Flexible, with one internal K-E salt bridge. The charge pair makes the segment less likely to collapse back onto the scaffold and slightly more resistant to proteases than a pure Gly-Ser run. It sits below the neutral Gly-Ser entries for that reason: two charged residues next to the fusion are one more thing a peptide whose activity depends on local charge or on a hydrophobic patch has to tolerate.

name: (GGS)₃
description: Triplet GGS flexible unit — even smaller periodic than GGGGS, used where minimal side-chain bulk is needed. Each unit is 3 aa so the construct stays very compact.
reference: Crasto & Feng 2000, Proteins: Structure, Function, and Bioinformatics.
priority_reason: A smaller Gly-Gly-Ser period, three times over. The segment stays compact and adds little bulk while still separating the two domains, which suits a peptide that should sit close to the scaffold rather than far from it. The trade is a lower serine fraction than the GGGGS family: marginally less solubilising, marginally more prone to collapse.

name: (GGGGS)₃
description: Three tandem GGGGS units — a longer flexible linker used when the two domains need substantial spatial separation. Common in bispecific antibodies and cytokine fusion constructs.
priority_reason: Flexible at fifteen residues. It still separates cleanly, but it has left the useful window: every residue past about ten adds unstructured surface for proteases to cut and mass for the recombinant host to make. Reach for it when the peptide must sit clearly outside a large scaffold, not as a default.

name: (GGGGS)₄
description: Four tandem GGGGS units — long flexible linker reserved for cases where the two domains must be physically well-separated, such as when steric clash would otherwise mask binding sites.
priority_reason: The same argument at twenty residues — more reach, more open surface, a higher expression cost. Reserved for a case where a steric clash would otherwise mask the peptide's site.

name: (GGGGS)₅
description: Five tandem GGGGS units — the longest flexible linker in routine use. Often the upper bound for fusion protein linker length; beyond this, expression yield tends to drop sharply.
priority_reason: The longest flexible linker in routine use, and close to the upper bound; beyond this length recombinant yield tends to fall. Justified only when the two domains have to be physically far apart.

name: EAAAK
description: Single α-helical rigid unit — five residues fold into a stable helix that fixes inter-domain distance and orientation. E and K at the ends create salt bridges that cap the helix and minimise fraying.
reference: Waldo et al. 1999; Arai et al. 2001.
priority_reason: First of the rigid family. A single α-helical unit fixes the distance and the angle between the peptide and the scaffold, which is what you want when the geometry itself is the requirement — and not what you want when the peptide needs to adjust its own conformation to reach a target. Five residues is also a short leash for a large scaffold surface. The glutamate-lysine pair caps the helix and limits fraying.

name: (EAAAK)₃
description: Three tandem α-helical units — long rigid linker that maintains a strict ~22 Å inter-domain distance. Used when domains must remain conformationally isolated (e.g., to prevent allosteric interference).
reference: Arai et al. 2001; Chen et al. 2016, PMID 26394862.
priority_reason: Rigid at fifteen residues, roughly 22 Å of fixed separation. Choose it to hold the peptide at a set distance rather than to let it move. A helix is compact and its salt bridges are buried, so it is less protease-accessible than a flexible segment of the same length; the cost is a peptide whose orientation is decided for it.

name: (EAAAK)₄
description: Four tandem α-helical units — extended rigid linker for cases requiring strong spatial isolation between two folded domains over a >30 Å range.
priority_reason: Rigid at twenty residues, for cases that need strong spatial isolation between the two folded parts over a distance a flexible linker of tolerable length cannot guarantee.

name: (EAAAK)₅
description: Five tandem α-helical units — the longest rigid α-helical linker in routine use. The peptide forms a stable 5-turn helix; expression in E. coli is generally robust because of the high helical propensity.
priority_reason: The longest rigid α-helical linker in routine use — a five-turn helix. Worth noting that high helical propensity is generally well tolerated by E. coli, which is the one respect in which a long rigid linker is easier to produce than a long flexible one.

name: (AKEAAAKA)₂
description: Tandem AKEAAAKA rigid unit. Forms an even more stable α-helix than (EAAAK)n due to internal salt-bridge optimisation; favoured in crystallography work where rigid separation is critical.
priority_reason: Rigid, with the salt bridges rearranged for a more stable helix than EAAAK repeats of similar length. It is the most conformationally restrictive entry in the library: the right tool for holding two domains apart under all conditions, and the least forgiving if the peptide needs any mobility at all.

name: GPG
description: Classic β-turn unit — proline forces a tight turn, holding the two fused domains at a fixed angle. Often used to maintain a defined domain orientation.
priority_reason: Not a default. Proline forces a tight β-turn, giving the two domains a fixed relative angle at minimal length — the classic answer when the geometry must be locked and the peptide must stay close to the scaffold. Three residues cannot lift a peptide clear of a large scaffold surface, and proline-rich sequences are among the harder ones to express recombinantly. One place it is the natural choice is a collagen fusion, where the scaffold's polyproline-II helix and a proline turn are conformationally related.

name: SAP
description: Very short rigid linker — proline locks the backbone into a kink, separating two domains with minimal peptide burden. Often used in tag-fusion constructs.
priority_reason: The shortest rigid option after GPG: a proline kink with the least possible peptide burden, in use for tag fusions. It carries GPG's two limitations — too short to separate a peptide from a bulky scaffold, and proline-rich.

name: (P)₅
description: Polyproline helix — a fully rigid rod-like linker. Constrains the fused domains at a fixed distance but does not promote any inter-domain flexibility.
priority_reason: A polyproline rod. Fully rigid, no inter-domain flexibility at all, and the hardest of the fifteen to produce recombinantly. Last because it offers least of what this platform needs: a peptide that stays active on the outside of a structural protein.
